Equivalence classes of graphs arise in several settings, for instance, during
causal discovery algorithms. This guide covers the graph classes that represent
such classes and how to work with them.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(CausalStructures)
```

## Equivalence classes of DAGs

A PDAG (partially directed acyclic graph) is a graph whose edges may be directed
or undirected, with no directed cycles. Two DAGs are Markov equivalent if and
only if they have the same skeleton and the same v-structures (unshielded
colliders).

Each Markov equivalence class of DAGs has a unique CPDAG (completed partially
directed acyclic graph) representation. In a CPDAG, an edge is directed
precisely when it has the same orientation in every DAG in the equivalence
class; otherwise it remains undirected.

Given a DAG, `dag_to_cpdag()` computes its CPDAG:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

dag <- cgraph(C %-->% X, A %-->% X + Y, Y %-->% Z)
cpdag <- dag_to_cpdag(dag)
plot(cpdag)
```

The v-structure `C --> X <-- A` appears in every DAG in the equivalence class
and therefore remains directed. The edges `A --- Y` and `Y --- Z` are undirected
because no v-structure or Meek rule forces their orientation.

`count_dags()` tells us how many DAGs are in the class, and `enumerate_dags()`
lists them all:

```{r}
count_dags(cpdag)
```

```{r}
enumerate_dags(cpdag)
```

When you need one concrete DAG to work with, `dag_from_pdag()` picks one:

```{r}
dag_from_pdag(cpdag)
```

You can compute adjustment sets on a CPDAG, and the result is valid for every
DAG in the equivalence class:

```{r}
all_adjustment_sets(cpdag, "X", "Z")
```

An MPDAG (maximally oriented partially directed acyclic graph) can, for
instance, arise when background knowledge is incorporated during causal
discovery, orienting some edges of a CPDAG.

`meek_closure()` propagates all further orientations implied by Meek's rules on
a PDAG to obtain an MPDAG:

```{r}
pdag <- cgraph(C %---% X, A %-->% X, A %---% Y, Y %-->% Z, class = "PDAG")
mpdag <- meek_closure(pdag)
mpdag
```

Here, `X --- C` was oriented to `X --> C` using Meek's rules.

All the functions shown above work on any PDAG, CPDAG or MPDAG:

```{r}
count_dags(pdag)
all_adjustment_sets(mpdag, "X", "Z")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Only CPDAGs are guaranteed to be extendable"}
Every CPDAG represents a non-empty Markov equivalence class, so it always admits
at least one consistent DAG extension and `dag_from_pdag()` is guaranteed to
succeed. This is not true for a general PDAG or MPDAG: being acyclic (and, for
an MPDAG, closed under Meek's rules) is not sufficient to ensure a consistent
extension exists. For example, a chordless undirected cycle is a valid PDAG and
MPDAG, yet it cannot be oriented into a DAG without introducing a new
v-structure:

```{r}
#| error: true

cg <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C %---% D %---% A, class = "PDAG")
is_cpdag(cg)
is_mpdag(cg)
dag_from_pdag(cg)
```
:::

## Equivalence classes of MAGs

Maximal ancestral graphs (MAGs) naturally arise when some common causes are
unobserved: every latent common cause between two observed nodes becomes a
bidirected edge (`<->`) in the MAG. Two MAGs are Markov equivalent if they
encode the same conditional independence structure over the observed variables.

Each Markov equivalence class of MAGs has a unique PAG (partial ancestral
graph). Like a CPDAG for DAGs, the PAG marks each endpoint with the symbol
shared by every MAG in the class. A circle (`o`) at an endpoint means that mark
is not invariant; some MAGs in the class have a tail there and others have an
arrowhead.

Consider a MAG where `A` and `B` share a hidden common cause, `C` directly
causes `B`, and `B` directly causes `D`:

```{r}
mag <- cgraph(A %<->% B, C %-->% B %-->% D, class = "MAG")
mag
```

`mag_to_pag()` computes the PAG representing the Markov equivalence class of
this MAG, so all MAGs that encode the same conditional independences:

```{r}
pag <- mag_to_pag(mag)
pag
```

The arrowheads at `B` on the `A`-`B` and `C`-`B` edges are invariant: `A`, `B`,
and `C` form an unshielded collider at `B` (since `A` and `C` are non-adjacent),
so every MAG in the class has an edge pointing into `B` from both sides. The
circle marks at `A` and `C` are not invariant; the `A`-`B` edge could be
`A --> B` or `A <-> B`, and similarly for `C`. The `B --> D` edge is invariant
via Zhang's orientation rule R1: since `A` and `D` are non-adjacent and
`A o-> B --> D`, the tail at `B` is forced in all MAGs.

`enumerate_mags()` lets you explore the equivalence class:

```{r}
enumerate_mags(pag)
```

You can also answer various causal inference questions, see [PAG Causal
Effects](pag-causal-effects.qmd) for some examples.
